title: Electron Spin, Box Notation and Shell Mapping
topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: Spin quantum number and the box-arrow notation, mapped onto the shell structure — the drawing skills needed for configuration and orbital-diagram questions.

mₛ = +½ (↑) or −½ (↓) for every electron, independent of n, l, m. Spin angular momentum is √(3/4)ħ. Consequences: an orbital holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli); a shell holds 2n²; a subshell holds 2(2l + 1).
• One box per orbital; label the subshell above (2p: three boxes).
• Aufbau: fill orbitals in increasing (n + l) order.
• Hund: in degenerate boxes, one up-arrow per box before any pairing.
• Pauli: two arrows in one box must be opposite (↑↓).

Unpaired electrons → paramagnetism, μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM; paired → diamagnetic. The diagram also shows why carbon forms two covalent bonds after promotion (two half-filled p orbitals) and why the noble gases are inert (all boxes paired).
confusion: ❌ Arrows in the same box may point the same way. ✅ Pauli forbids it — opposite spins only.
❌ Pairing starts in the first p box. ✅ Hund's rule: each degenerate box gets one electron first.
❌ Spin affects the shape of orbitals. ✅ Spin changes capacity and magnetism, not the shape given by l.

summary: Spin mₛ = ±½ applies to every electron regardless of n, l or m, and its angular momentum is √3/4 ħ; its consequences are that an orbital holds at most two electrons (Pauli), a subshell 2(2l + 1) and a shell 2n². Box notation encodes the three rules: one box per orbital labelled with its subshell, orbitals filled in increasing (n + l) order (Aufbau), one up-arrow in each degenerate box before any pairing (Hund), and only opposite arrows in a filled box (Pauli). Mapping orbitals onto shells gives K = 1s (2e⁻), L = 2s + 2p (8), M = 3s + 3p + 3d (18) and N = 4s + 4p + 4d + 4f (32). Worked diagrams — N: 2p ↑ ↑ ↑, O: 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑, Cr: 3d ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ with 4s ↑ — lead directly to unpaired-electron counts, paramagnetism with μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM, carbon's two bonds after promotion, and the inertness of noble gases.
importantConcepts: Spin mₛ = ±½ for every electron, independent of n, l and m, with angular momentum √3/4 ħ
Box notation rules: one box per orbital, (n + l) filling order, parallel arrows first, opposite arrows only when paired
Shell mapping: K 1s (2), L 2s + 2p (8), M 3s + 3p + 3d (18), N 4s + 4p + 4d + 4f (32)
Worked diagrams: N 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ (3 unpaired), O 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑ (2 unpaired), Cr 3d⁵4s¹ (half-filled)
Unpaired electrons give paramagnetism with μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM; fully paired species are diamagnetic
importantStatements: Two arrows in one box must point in opposite directions — Pauli forbids parallel spins in one orbital.
Pairing begins only after every degenerate box of the subshell holds one electron (Hund's rule).
Spin changes capacity and magnetism, never the orbital shape, which is fixed by l.
The 4s orbital fills before 3d but empties first on ion formation.
Nitrogen's three unpaired 2p electrons explain its paramagnetism and its tendency to form a triple bond.

keyPoints: Box diagrams are also called orbital diagrams; the arrows denote mₛ = ±½.
Always draw separate boxes for degenerate orbitals — merging them loses the Hund's rule marks.
μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM, so V (3d³, u = 3) gives √15 ≈ 3.87 BM.
Paired electrons in every box = diamagnetic; any unpaired electron = paramagnetic.
specialNotes: A half-filled or fully filled subshell in a box diagram signals extra stability, as in Cr ([Ar]3d⁵4s¹).
Box diagrams show the ground state; promotion to 2s for carbon happens only when bonds form.
The number of orbitals, not the number of electrons, is what Hund's rule counts.
examShortTricks: Fill boxes in the order one arrow each, then pair — this reproduces Hund's rule mechanically.
Relate the unpaired-electron count directly to magnetic behaviour in the last line of the answer.
For transition metals remember 4s empties before 3d when ions form.
